> Friday 17 July 2026 — biomarker discovery, integration sites, viral evolution,
> phylogenetics. Two hands-on practicals; the rest is pen, paper, and argument.

## How this works

The exercises are grouped by facilitator and follow Day 2's
[schedule](index.qmd#schedule). Each section **leads with its hands-on
practical**, then the discussion exercises for that facilitator's sessions.

**[Dr. Malika Aid Boudries](#prof-malika)** opens with integration sites and ATAC-seq in R
([Exercise 1](#exercise-1)). Her remaining exercises are discussion-based.

**[Dr. Choga](#dr-choga)** closes the day with two hands-on practicals — the
mutations and minority-variants analysis ([Exercise 6](#exercise-6)) and the
phylogenetics practical ([Exercise 7](#exercise-7)), alignment to time-scaled
tree in IQ-TREE and TreeTime — plus two discussion exercises.

::: {.callout-important}
## The practicals need setup — do it before the session
Exercises 1, 6 and 7 each need software installed and files downloaded.
Conference wifi will not save you. See
[Installation](installation-instructions.qmd), and the setup steps in each
exercise.
:::

Every discussion exercise asks the same three questions:

1. What does this result actually say?
2. What would you do next?
3. **What could go wrong?**

Question 3 is still the one that matters. Work in pairs, roughly 15 minutes
each, then we discuss as a group.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Day 1's lesson still applies
A method always returns an answer. On Day 2 the methods are more elaborate —
DESeq2, GSEA, GRanges, IQ-TREE, BEAST — which means they return answers that
*look* more authoritative. That is a reason for more suspicion, not less.
:::

# Dr. Malika Aid Boudries {#prof-malika}

## Exercise 1 — SIV Integration Sites & ATAC-seq in R {#exercise-1}

*Session: SIV/HIV integration site profiling · 11:30 · hands-on in RStudio*

Materials prepared by **Aisha Olufayo** (Research Intern, Boudries Lab, CVVR) —
[aolufayo@bidmc.harvard.edu](mailto:aolufayo@bidmc.harvard.edu).

You will annotate simulated SIV integration sites, then overlap them with
simulated ATAC-seq peaks to ask whether the virus integrates into open
chromatin.

### Get the workshop files

Go to the workshop repository, click the green **CODE** button, then
**Download ZIP**:

[{{< fa brands github >}} aolufayo-bidmc/IS-ATAC-Workshop](https://github.com/aolufayo-bidmc/IS-ATAC-Workshop){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}
[{{< fa file-pdf >}} Getting Started (PDF)](assets/day2/IS-ATAC-getting-started.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-secondary target="_blank"}

Unzip it somewhere you can find again. The package contains **simulated
integration site data** and **simulated ATAC-peak data** — no participant data
is involved.

::: {.callout-note}
## This is a live repository
The code is maintained and may be updated before the session. If you downloaded
the ZIP well in advance, **download it again the night before** so you have the
current version.
:::

### Prerequisites

- **R** — version 4.4 or later recommended
- **RStudio Desktop**

Both are already on the [Installation](installation-instructions.qmd) list for
this workshop.

### Install the R packages

Paste this into your R console. It checks for each package and installs only
what is missing:

```r
packages <- c("tidyverse", "readxl", "writexl", "openxlsx", "readr", "BiocManager")

for (pkg in packages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Step 0 — do not skip this
Open the R project file **`IS_ATAC_Workshop_Files.Rproj`** first, and work from
the Files pane inside that project.

This puts RStudio in the correct working directory. Filenames are written
directly into the scripts for convenience, so opening the `.R` files any other
way means **the code will not find its inputs**. Nearly every problem in this
session traces back to this step.
:::

### The run order

| | Step | What you do | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cleaning up the integration site file | **No action** — follow the live demonstration | `Simulated_IS_clean.xlsx` |
| 2 | Annotating SIV integration sites | Open and run `2. Annotate Insertion Sites.R` | `Simulated_IS_annotated.xlsx` → `outputs/` |
| 3 | Overlapping IS with open chromatin | Open and run `3. Alignment of ATAC-seq data with IS data.R` | `Simulated_IS_openchr.xlsx` → `inputs/` |
| 4 | Annotating IS in open chromatin | Open and run `4. Annotating Overlap Sites.R` | `Simulated_IS_openchr_annotated.xlsx` → `outputs/` |

**Step 1** is a demonstration of the cleaning process that gets raw integration
sites into the shape everything else expects. You do not need to open any files
or run this yourself — watch, and understand what the cleaning did, because it
is where the judgement calls are.

**Step 2** takes the cleaned data and annotates each insertion site: the gene it
lands in, its location within that gene, the surrounding sequence.

**Step 3** is the conceptual core. Both the integration sites and the ATAC-seq
peaks are converted to **GRanges** objects, and `subsetByOverlaps()` finds the
integration sites sharing **at least one base pair** with a region of open
chromatin.

**Step 4** annotates those overlapping sites exactly as in step 2, giving you
the integration sites that fall in open chromatin, with genes attached.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If a script does not run
Each step eats the previous step's output, so a failure is almost always a
missing input:

- **Step 2 fails?** Check `Simulated_IS_clean.xlsx` is in your `inputs` folder.
- **Step 4 fails?** Check `Simulated_IS_openchr.xlsx` is in your `inputs` folder.
- **Anything fails immediately?** You probably did not open the `.Rproj` file.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Further instructions
The ZIP contains a fuller instructions file — the same
[Getting Started guide](assets/day2/IS-ATAC-getting-started.pdf) linked above.
You do not need it until we walk through the session live. Bring it installed
and downloaded; we will do the rest together.
:::

### While you run it, think about

- `subsetByOverlaps()` accepts an overlap of **one base pair**. Is one base pair
  a biologically meaningful definition of "integrated into open chromatin"?
- What would the result look like if SIV integrated *completely at random*?
  Exercise 2 is that question.

## Exercise 2 — An integration site hotspot

*Session: SIV/HIV integration site profiling · 11:30 · pen and paper*

Exercise 1 gave you overlaps. This one asks whether you should believe them.

You map integration sites in a real dataset and find a striking result: **31% of
all sites** fall in one gene, *BACH2*. The clonal expansion literature makes
this exciting — a selected, persistently infected clone.

- What would convince you this is real?
- What is the alternative explanation?
- What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Discussion
**Ask what "31% of sites" is counting.** If it counts *sequencing reads*, you
have measured PCR amplification, not biology. One efficiently amplified template
can dominate a library. Integration site work counts **unique** sites —
deduplicated by breakpoint, ideally with sonication- or UMI-based fragment
tagging — for exactly this reason.

**The alternative explanation is the pipeline.** Before biology, rule out
mapping ambiguity in repetitive regions and a contaminating index-hopped
sample. Then rule out the null: integration is **not uniform to begin with**.
HIV/SIV favour actively transcribed, accessible chromatin — which is the entire
premise of Exercise 1. "Found in a transcribed gene" is therefore the
expectation, not the discovery.

**This is why the overlap in Exercise 1 needs a control.** A percentage of sites
in open chromatin means nothing on its own. It only means something against a
**matched random control** — sites shuffled while preserving whatever structure
you are not testing — because comparing your observed overlap to an implicit
assumption of uniformity will make even random data look enriched.

**What would convince you:** the same site recovered from independent samples
and independent library preps; an enrichment test against that matched control;
and a clone size estimated from unique breakpoints, not reads.

**What could go wrong:** *BACH2* is a genuine, well-documented clonal expansion
hotspot. That is what makes this trap effective — the literature will happily
confirm a result your pipeline manufactured. A finding that matches expectation
gets less scrutiny, and needs more.
:::

## Exercise 3 — Reading a DESeq2 result

*Session: Biomarker discovery using bulk RNA-Seq · 9:00*

You run the Week 24 contrast from the
[bulk RNA-Seq session](materials/3-bulk-rnaseq/index.qmd). Out of 18,285 genes,
just over 400 come back with an adjusted p-value below 0.05. One of them looks
like this:

```
gene      baseMean   log2FoldChange   lfcSE   padj
GENE_X       7.4          3.9          1.1    0.021
```

- What does the sign of that fold change mean here?
- Is this a biomarker candidate?
- What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Discussion
**The sign first.** `Status` is forced to `c("NoRebound", "Rebound")`, so the
contrast is Rebound vs NoRebound and a **positive** `log2FoldChange` means
higher in **Rebound**. GENE_X is roughly 15-fold up in rebounders. If you got
that backwards, every sentence you write about this gene is inverted.

**Is it a candidate?** Look at `baseMean` before you get excited. A mean of 7.4
counts across the samples is close to nothing — this gene is barely detected.
Large fold changes are *easy* at low counts, because the ratio of two small
noisy numbers is unstable. That is why DESeq2 shrinks fold changes, and why an
`lfcSE` of 1.1 is telling you the estimate is soft.

**What could go wrong:** ranking by `log2FoldChange` puts low-expression noise
at the top of your list. Rank by adjusted p-value, or filter on `baseMean`
first, and look at the MA plot — the fan of large effects at the left edge is
this artifact, drawn.

Also: 400 hits out of 18,285 at 5% FDR means roughly 20 are expected to be false
positives. Not "the list is wrong", but "the list contains false positives by
construction, and I do not know which".
:::

---

## Exercise 4 — GSEA and the tempting pathway

*Session: Biomarker discovery using bulk RNA-Seq · 9:00*

You run GSEA against the 50 MSigDB Hallmark sets.
`HALLMARK_INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE` comes back strongly enriched in rebounders,
FDR < 0.001. It is an immunologically satisfying result: interferon signalling,
in a viral rebound study.

- Does this tell you interferon signalling causes rebound?
- What is GSEA actually testing?
- What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Discussion
**No.** GSEA tests whether genes in a set sit higher in your ranked list than
chance would put them. It is a statement about **coordinated ranking** — not
mechanism, not direction of causation, not timing.

**What could go wrong:** several things at once.

*The satisfying result is the dangerous one.* Interferon response is one of the
most commonly enriched Hallmark sets in any dataset involving virus, infection,
or inflammation. Its appearance is weakly informative. You would have accepted
it without question — which is precisely why you should question it.

*Hallmark sets overlap.* Genes appear in several sets, so "five enriched
pathways" may be one signal counted five times. That is what the
`Organize_Significant_GSEA_Pathways_into_Modules.R` script exists to expose.

*Direction is inherited from the contrast.* If you flipped the factor levels in
Exercise 3, this enrichment flips with it.

*Correlation with rebound is not prediction of rebound.* The
[ML session](materials/2-ml-session/index.qmd) asks the prediction question, and
it is a different question with a different answer.
:::

---

## Exercise 5 — Cells, or observations?

*Session: Single cell multiome profiling in CD4 T cells · 10:15*

A colleague profiles CD4 T cells from **4 SIV-infected macaques** and 4
controls. After QC they have 40,000 cells. They run a differential expression
test across cells, infected vs control, and report genes at p < 10⁻³⁰⁰.

- Why is that p-value so small?
- What is the sample size in this study?
- What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Discussion
**n = 8, not 40,000.** This is pseudoreplication, and it is the single most
common error in single-cell work.

Cells from one animal are not independent observations of "SIV infection". They
share that animal's genotype, viral load, treatment history, tissue handling,
and the batch it was processed in. Testing across 40,000 cells asks "do cells
differ?" while the biological question is "do *animals* differ?" — and the test
answers the question you asked, with enormous confidence, because 40,000 is a
big number.

**That p-value is a measure of cell count, not evidence.** With enough cells you
can drive any p-value arbitrarily low, including for a gene whose difference is
driven entirely by one animal.

**What to do instead:** pseudobulk. Aggregate counts per animal per cell type,
then test across the 8 animals with DESeq2 — the same tool from Exercise 3. You
will get far fewer hits and far larger error bars, and that is the honest
picture. Four versus four is a small study; the analysis should say so.

**What could still go wrong:** with n=4 per group, one outlier animal is 25% of
its group. Plot per-animal values for every gene you intend to report. If the
signal is one macaque, you have found one macaque.
:::

# Dr. Choga {#dr-choga}

## Exercise 6 — Mutations, Diversity, Burden & Minority Variants {#exercise-6}

*Session: Principles of Viral Evolution · 13:45 · hands-on in R*

The first of the afternoon's two practicals. You work a whole-genome HIV-1
deep-sequencing sample from raw per-position pileup all the way to minority
variants, diversity, and a burden test — using **real** data from a single
patient.

### Get the practical

[{{< fa file-zipper >}} Download the workshop (ZIP)](materials/6-mutations/mutations_workshop.zip){.btn .btn-primary}
[{{< fa file-lines >}} Rendered report (HTML)](materials/6-mutations/mutations_workshop.html){.btn .btn-outline-secondary target="_blank"}
[{{< fa chalkboard >}} Slides](materials/6-mutations/slides.html){.btn .btn-outline-secondary target="_blank"}

The analysis is a single R Markdown document, `mutations_workshop.Rmd`. Open it
in RStudio and run it top to bottom — **every number in the prose is computed
from the data, not typed in**, so a clean run reproduces the whole argument.

**Needs:** R, RStudio, and the packages `tidyverse`, `patchwork`, `knitr`.

::: {.callout-note}
## The data is real, and de-identified
This is a genuine HIV-1 sample aligned to **NC_001802.1** — not a simulation.
The original sample barcode has been removed from the filename and every
sequence header; the pileup itself carries only positions and base counts, no
identifiers. Treat it as you would any patient-derived sequence: the numbers are
for learning the method, not for reporting as a clinical result.
:::

### The reversal is the point

::: {.callout-important}
## A confident, significant result that is an artefact
Partway through, the naive minority-variant analysis — a 1% VAF threshold with a
binomial test against the error rate — produces an **FDR-significant** result.
It is wrong. It is a sequencing artefact, and the binomial test cannot see it.

You will catch it with a **Ti/Tv stress test**, diagnose it from the
**substitution spectrum**, fix it by filtering the artefact signature, and then
*validate the fix biologically* against the **APOBEC3G** editing signature. That
catch-diagnose-fix-validate loop is the whole workshop. A p-value below your
threshold is where the thinking starts, not where it ends.
:::

### What you build, in order

| Section | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Dataset & QC | FASTQ-style pileup, coverage QC before any calling |
| What a mutation is | Consensus (ref vs strain) vs within-host variation |
| Types of mutation | Structural, Ti/Tv, coding effect, origin |
| Calculating them | Allele frequency (VAF) — and why frequency ≠ rate |
| Diversity | Shannon entropy per site, nucleotide diversity π, per-gene |
| **Minority variants** | The naive call, the artefact, the fix, APOBEC validation |
| Burden testing | Regional enrichment, then a simulated case/control cohort |

::: {.callout-note}
## An honest note carried from the workshop
A classical burden test compares cases vs controls across **many individuals**.
This is **one sample**, so you cannot run one — and the document says so plainly.
What you *can* run is the same machinery in its within-sample form (regional
enrichment), then a *simulated* cohort for the case/control version. Being clear
about what a single sample can and cannot support is itself part of the lesson.
:::

### The `pol` and `env` minority-variant sets

The ZIP also ships translated and nucleotide minority-variant FASTAs for the
**`pol`** (PR, RT, IN) and **`env`** genes across a threshold sweep
(5%–50%), built by `pol_minority_fasta.R` and `env_minority_fasta.R`. These feed
the threshold-comparison figures and let you see how the variant set shrinks as
you demand more evidence — the same "where do I set the line?" question the
minority-variant section answers for the whole genome.

## Exercise 7 — Practical 2: Molecular Evolution & Phylogenetics {#exercise-7}

*Sessions: Principles of Viral Evolution · 13:45 — and Phylogenetics &
Phylodynamics · 15:30 · hands-on*

The main practical for the afternoon: from a sequence alignment to a
time-scaled phylogeny, and — the actual point — to deciding whether to believe
it.

### Get the practical

[{{< fa file-zipper >}} Download the workshop (ZIP)](materials/6-phylogenetics-practical/Phylogenetics_Workshop.zip){.btn .btn-primary}
[{{< fa book >}} Workshop Manual](materials/6-phylogenetics-practical/notes/WORKSHOP_MANUAL.md){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}
[{{< fa compass >}} Interpretation Guide](materials/6-phylogenetics-practical/notes/INTERPRETATION_GUIDE.md){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}
[{{< fa database >}} Data Provenance](materials/6-phylogenetics-practical/data/README_DATA.md){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-secondary}

Unzip it, and run everything **from the workshop folder** — not from inside
`scripts/`.

```bash
cd Phylogenetics_Workshop
bash run_all.sh          # regenerates every result and figure (~10 min)
```

Every script takes a dataset argument — `sim` or `h1n1`:

```bash
Rscript scripts/04_root_to_tip.R h1n1
```

**Needs:** `Rscript`, `iqtree2`, `treetime`, `python3` — plus the R packages
Biostrings, ape, phangorn, phytools, treeio, ggtree, ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr,
readr, ggrepel, scales, lubridate.

::: {.callout-note}
## The figures and results are already in the ZIP
If your install is not cooperating, you can still follow every exercise — the
generated `figures/` and `results/` ship with it. `run_all.sh` regenerates them
from scratch when you are ready.
:::

### Two datasets that disagree

This is the design. Most practicals hand you one dataset that works, everything
succeeds, and you learn nothing about judgement.

| | **B — simulated** | **C — 2009 pandemic H1N1** |
|---|---|---|
| **What** | Simulated HIV-like epidemic | **Real** influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 genomes |
| **Size** | 60 seq × 1,500 bp | 50 genomes × 13,109 bp |
| **Sampled over** | **20 years** (2005–2025) | **43 days** (Apr–May 2009) |
| **Truth** | **Known** — rate 2.2×10⁻³, tMRCA 1992.7 | Compare to published estimates |
| **Temporal signal** | R² ≈ **0.80** → "trust it" | R² ≈ **0.20** → "weak signal" |
| **Outcome** | Recovers the truth | **Recovers the truth anyway** |

Dataset C scores *very weak* on every R² lookup table you will find — and then
returns a textbook pandemic H1N1 rate and a tMRCA matching the published 2009
origin to within weeks.

::: {.callout-important}
## That contradiction is the workshop
Dataset C's R² is low **only because 43 days of sampling gives the regression
nothing to lever against**. Low R² is a *symptom, not a diagnosis*. Read the
lookup table without asking *why*, and you throw away a perfectly good analysis.

This is Exercise 9's lesson from the other direction: there a narrow output is
wrong; here a discouraging one is right. **Neither number can be read without
knowing where it came from.**
:::

### The 15 exercises

| | Exercise | Script |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Inspect the alignment — length, Ns, duplicates, variable sites | `01_inspect_alignment.R` |
| 2 | Build the ML tree — bootstrap + SH-aLRT | `02_run_iqtree.sh` |
| 3–4 | Visualise and root the tree | `03_plot_ml_tree.R` |
| 5–6 | Root-to-tip regression, then **interpret it** | `04_root_to_tip.R` |
| 7–8 | TreeTime — the time-scaled phylogeny | `05_run_treetime.sh` |
| 9–10, 12–13 | tMRCA, ggtree, publication figure, metadata | `06_timetree_ggtree.R` |
| 11 | The molecular clock vs published ranges | `07_clock_summary.R` |
| 14 | Cluster detection + threshold sweep | `08_clusters.R` |
| 15 | Final interpretation | — |

Exercise 6 is the hinge. Everything before it produces numbers; Exercise 6 is
where you decide what they mean.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Dataset B has a planted error
`SIM_dates.tsv` contains one deliberately wrong date. Exercise 5 is where it
surfaces — as a residual that does not belong. Finding it is the exercise;
`SIM_truth.txt` confirms it once you have.
:::

### The optional negative control

A third dataset — **real HIV-1 *gag*** from six African countries — is not built
by default. Build it with `python3 scripts/00a_prepare_hiv.py` if you have the
source file.

It is the negative control, and it is brutal: unlinked cross-sectional HIV from
a mature epidemic has almost no temporal signal (R² ≈ 0.06), because two random
subtype-C patients differ by ~0.145 subs/site while 20 years of clock evolution
adds only ~0.02. TreeTime dates its ancestor to **1793** — centuries before
HIV-1 group M entered humans — **without a single warning.**

::: {.callout-important}
## Read the data provenance before quoting any number
In the HIV dataset, `country`, `year` and `gene` are real; sample identifiers
have been **re-issued** so no patient or study identifier appears. But
`province`, `risk_group` and `subtype` are **fabricated** — they exist so
Exercise 13 has something to colour by. Never analyse them as data, and never
let them leave the workshop attached to these sequences.

And a phylogenetic cluster is **not** evidence that one person infected another.
Inferred linkage has been misused in criminal prosecutions. That belongs
alongside the method, not after it.
:::

## Exercise 8 — The alignment you did not look at

*Session: Principles of Viral Evolution · 13:45 · AliView + RStudio*

You have 60 HBV sequences, align them, and open the alignment in AliView. The
first and last ~200 columns are ragged and gap-rich. A few sequences have long
runs of `N`. One sequence is 400 bp shorter than everything else.

You are about to hand this to IQ-TREE.

- Which of these actually matters?
- What do you do first?
- What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Discussion
**All of it matters, and none of it will stop the tree from being built.** That
is the point of this exercise.

**Do first:** look at it. You already are — that is the exercise. Then trim the
ragged ends, because those columns are not homologous; they are where coverage
ran out. Decide what to do about the `N` runs (they are missing data, and a
sequence that is 30% `N` contributes almost nothing but will still be placed on
the tree, usually somewhere flattering). Ask why one sequence is short before
you keep it.

**The circular genome.** HBV's genome is circular, so a linear alignment has an
arbitrary breakpoint, and sequences that start at different coordinates will
misalign catastrophically at the ends. Confirm every sequence uses the same
origin.

**What could go wrong:** every downstream inference. Tree-building assumes
column *i* is homologous across all sequences. Break that assumption and the
tree is still returned, still has branch lengths, and still looks entirely
reasonable — see
[Module 4](materials/3-bioinformatics-application/4-phylogenetics.qmd).

**And recombination.** HBV recombines. A tree assumes one history for the whole
alignment. If part of your alignment has a different history than the rest, no
single tree is correct, and the software will not tell you — it will average the
conflict into a confident-looking topology. Screen for recombination *before*
you build the tree, not after a reviewer asks.
:::

---

## Exercise 9 — A dated tree that is too good

*Session: Principles of Phylogenetics & Phylodynamics · 15:30 · IQ-TREE, FigTree, BEAST*

You build an ML tree in IQ-TREE, open it in FigTree, and a clade of 12 Botswana
sequences has **bootstrap 98**. Encouraged, you run BEAST on the same alignment
with a strict clock and estimate the most recent common ancestor at **1987
(95% HPD: 1985–1989)**.

Your sequences were all collected in a single year.

- What does bootstrap 98 mean here?
- Do you believe that date?
- What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Discussion
**Bootstrap first.** Bootstrap 98 means: resample the alignment columns, rebuild
the tree, and this clade reappears 98% of the time. It measures whether your
data **consistently** support the split. It does **not** measure whether the
split is true. A systematic error — misalignment, a recombinant, an unmodelled
substitution process — is present in every resample, so it is supported at 98%
too. **Bootstrap measures precision, not accuracy.** Consistent and wrong is an
available outcome, and it is the one Exercise 8 sets you up for.

**The date: no.** Tip-dated molecular clock inference gets its calibration from
*variation in sampling times*. All sequences from one year means there is no
temporal signal to estimate a rate from — the rate is coming from your prior,
and BEAST will hand back a posterior with a tight, entirely fictional HPD. A
narrow credible interval is not evidence; it is what a confident prior looks
like after it has been passed through a likelihood that contained no information
about the parameter.

**Check for temporal signal before you run BEAST** — a root-to-tip regression in
TempEst. Flat or negative slope means stop.

**What else could go wrong:** the strict clock assumes one rate across the whole
tree — test whether a relaxed clock fits better rather than assuming. And the
tree prior is not a formality: a coalescent prior encodes assumptions about
population history that will shape your dates.

::: {.callout-important}
## The pattern across both exercises
Bootstrap 98 and an HPD of ±2 years are both **narrow outputs**. Neither is
evidence of correctness. Software reports uncertainty *within* its assumptions;
it has no way to report that the assumptions were wrong.
:::
:::

---

## Wrapping up

Across Day 2, tracking every session:

- Two failures came from **counting the wrong unit** — reads instead of
  templates (2), cells instead of animals (5).
- Two came from **trusting an output whose narrowness was manufactured** —
  bootstrap 98 and a 4-year HPD from sequences with no temporal signal (9).
- One came from a **significant p-value that was a sequencing artefact** — caught
  only by a stress test the binomial never applied (6).
- One came from **not looking at the input** (8).
- One came from a result being **too satisfying to interrogate** (4).
- And one — the overlap in Exercise 1 — is **uninterpretable without a control**,
  which is the whole of Exercise 2.

Not one of them was an algorithm failing. Every method ran correctly and
returned exactly what it was asked for.

And then Exercise 7 turns the whole thing around. Dataset C's R² of 0.20 says
*discard this*, and the analysis is sound. Dataset A's tree carries no warning
at all, and dates HIV to 1793. **A discouraging number is not a verdict, and a
confident one is not a licence** — you have to know why the number is what it
is. Reading either off a lookup table gets you the wrong answer in opposite
directions.

::: {.callout-important}
## The point
Day 1 asked whether your question could be answered by your data. Day 2 asks the
same question of more sophisticated tools, and the answer is the same: the
methods do not know what your samples are, whether your alignment is homologous,
whether one base pair of overlap means anything, or that HIV did not exist in
1793. **You are the only part of the pipeline that can check.**
:::
